messages.author: 9dd18974ee4e2aeb
messages.subject: Slow userGWAS function
parts:
Hi all, I'm new to genomicSEM and I've been trying to recreate some results I read in a research paper on two traits. I've successfully executed the prior steps but when I use the userGWAS function it's extremely slow and never seems to finish (I stopped when it hit 3 full days running). I set parallel = TRUE and used 30 cores of a server.

To troubleshoot I cut the summary statistics to 1 million snps each and used the same 30 cores, expecting it to take a lot less time, but it's been a full day and no sign of finishing.

I'm not sure if this is due to poor model fit or convergence or something else. I want to set the factor loadings for both traits to be equal, as the authors describe in the paper:

# Define the commonfactor model                                                                                                commonfactor.model <- 'F1 =~ a*ADHD + a*ASD 
F1 ~~ F1 
F1 ~ SNP'  
                  
# Run the commonfactorGWAS function                                                                        PSYCH_factor <- userGWAS(covstruc = LDSCoutput, SNPs = PSYCH_sumstats, estimation = "DWLS", model = commonfactor.model, cores = 30, parallel = TRUE)

When I remove the constraints from the model it gives me an error and using the commonfactorGWAS() function it also keeps running on on.

Thanks for any tips

messages.author: 3b39745f73eec779
messages.subject: Re: Slow userGWAS function
parts:
Speed can depend on a few factors, how long do 1000 SNPs take? 

There is this bit of context on the genomicSEM wiki that may help:

“
note on serial versus parallel processing. Serial and parallel processing will return the same output, but are computationally implemented in a serial and parallel fashion, respectively. In our experience using high performance computing systems there were often memory issues when using parallel processing (unless you have access to large memory nodes), in which case serial processing may be preferred. However, on a personal laptop with multiple cores, the computing time will be reduced greatly when using parallel processing. We note that each run is independent of one another, so it is also appropriate to set-up your runs in separate batches. The function runs as many models as there are SNPs.
”

So might be a memory issue? Things like chunking per chromosome or even smaller may reduce memory footprint, greatly speed things up and allow for faster parallel analysis.

Generally troubleshoot with 1000 SNPs and when things are smooth and fast scale up. I think think this should take 3 days.


Best,
Michel
